wins.need: Running 240 V appliances (well pump, central AC, dryer circuits) from one unit through a transfer switch
wins.claim: The highest rated 240 V output of the single units checked. It beats the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (6,000 W), the Anker SOLIX S5000 (4,500 W, supplying both 120 V and 240 V) and the BLUETTI Apex 300 (3,840 W).
wins.figure: 7,200 W max on L14-30R / L14-50R at 240 V (maker). F3800 Plus 6,000 W (ankersolix.com). S5000 4,500 W (pv magazine, Anker figure). Apex 300 3,840 W (bluettipower.com product title)
wins.who: Jackery spec sheet; rival figures from https://www.ankersolix.com/us/products/f3800-plus, https://now.solar/2026/10/28/anker-solix-s5000-deep-dive-review-5-kwh-on-wheels-tested-through-a-real-power-outage-pv-magazine-usa/ and https://www.bluettipower.com/products/apex-300-home-battery-backup

wins.need: Holding near full load at both voltages
wins.claim: HOBOTECH measured it holding its full rated output in a 5-minute heat test at both voltages, and briefly carrying surge loads well above rated.
wins.figure: Passed 3,600 W at 120 V and 7,200 W at 240 V for 5 minutes. Surge reached 4,800 W at 120 V and 9,300 W at 240 V for under 5 s

wins.need: More power from the ordinary 120 V outlets
wins.claim: Its paired 120 V outlets give more power than the F3800 Plus's standard 120 V outlets.
wins.figure: 3,600 W at 120 V/30 A from paired 5-20 outlets (AC1+AC2 or AC3+AC4), or 2,400 W from one outlet, vs 2,400 W from the F3800 Plus's standard 120 V outlets
wins.who: Jackery spec sheet; Anker figure from https://www.ankersolix.com/us/products/f3800-plus

wins.need: Fast solar recharging on a big array
wins.claim: It has the highest rated solar input of the rivals checked, and HOBOTECH measured more than 3,500 W.
wins.figure: 4,000 W high-voltage PV input (135–450 V, 15 A) vs 3,200 W for the F3800 Plus and 3,000 W for the S5000. HOBOTECH measured 3,500 W+ at 220 V and above, limited by their test equipment. Arithmetic: 5,040 Wh ÷ 4,000 W = 1.26 h at the ideal rate
wins.who: HOBOTECH measured; ratings from the Jackery FAQ spec sheet, ankersolix.com and pv magazine

wins.need: Lots of usable energy in one box
wins.claim: HOBOTECH measured about 4.45 kWh of usable AC energy from one unit. That is more than the full rated capacity of the F3800 Plus (3,840 Wh) or the Apex 300 (2,764.8 Wh) before their losses.

wins.need: Lower idle drain than Anker's F3800
wins.claim: The Solar Lab measured lower idle draw than the original Anker SOLIX F3800.
wins.figure: About 58 W vs 80 W for the F3800, inverter on, no load

weak.claim: High idle draw compared with the Anker SOLIX S5000 and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra. With the inverter left on, a day of idling uses a large share of the battery.
weak.figure: Measured 58 W (The Solar Lab) and 85 W (HOBOTECH: 515 Wh in 6 h). Jackery lists 50 W standby. S5000 measured about 10 W (pv magazine). DELTA Pro Ultra 52 W (cited by HOBOTECH). Arithmetic: 58 W × 24 h = 1,392 Wh, about 31% of HOBOTECH's measured 4,450 Wh usable

weak.claim: It struggled to start an air conditioner with a high start-up surge
weak.figure: Could not reliably start an AC unit with a 10,000 W surge. Ran 8,000 W and 9,500 W loads for 20–30 s

weak.claim: Charging at 240 V needs the optional Smart Transfer Switch. On a 120 V wall outlet it charges at about 1.75 kW.
weak.figure: Measured 1,750 W in fast mode and 1,400 W in quiet mode. Maker: 120 V, 15 A, 1,750 W ± 50 W

weak.claim: Heavy, and the extra batteries don't stack or roll with the main unit
weak.figure: About 61 kg (maker) vs 44 kg for the S5000 (pv magazine). HOBOTECH notes the packs don't stack or roll

weak.claim: The 50 A-style L14-50R outlet delivers 30 A
weak.figure: 7,200 W max at 240 V. Arithmetic: 7,200 ÷ 240 = 30 A. The Solar Lab lists 'the 50A plug supports only 30A' as a con

weak.claim: Less expansion headroom per unit than the F3800 Plus
weak.figure: Up to 5 packs (arithmetic: 6 × 5,040 Wh = 30.24 kWh) vs 53.8 kWh for the F3800 Plus
App drops its WiFi connection often. Only one 12 V socket. Low-voltage solar uses proprietary 8 mm inputs. 'Just don't get it wet.'

weak.claim: Costs more per kWh than its nearest rivals on Amazon and maker stores today (arithmetic)

wins_for: Homeowners who need real 240 V split-phase power (well pump, central AC, electric range or dryer circuits) from one portable unit through a transfer switch. It has the highest 240 V rating checked, and HOBOTECH measured it holding 7,200 W.
Outage backup with a large solar array. Its 4,000 W high-voltage solar input can refill the battery in a day of sun.
Shoppers searching the Jackery brand for whole-home backup. It is Jackery's largest single unit and the only Jackery checked with 240 V at 7,200 W.
Buyers who want room to grow, up to about 30 kWh per unit with Jackery packs (arithmetic from the maker's 5-pack limit)
not_for: Camping or RV use: it weighs about 61 kg and has a measured idle draw of 58–85 W. A smaller 1–2 kWh unit wins there.

Long outages on small loads such as a CPAP, fridge or router: idle draw of about 58 W can use more than the load itself. The Anker SOLIX S5000 wins, with about 10 W measured idle at similar capacity, $2,949 on Amazon (read 2026-11-15) and 44 kg.
Homes that only need 120 V: the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus (3,584 Wh, 3,600 W, $1,899 on Amazon, read 2026-11-15) costs less per kWh (arithmetic: $530 vs $694).
Starting a large central AC with a 10,000 W surge without a soft starter: The Solar Lab's unit struggled to start one.
Shoppers who want the most expansion on one unit: the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus expands to 53.8 kWh (Anker).

rivals.where_it_beats_ours: $550 cheaper on Amazon. Idle draw about 10 W, measured by Andrew Riha for pv magazine, vs 58 W measured by The Solar Lab. 44 kg vs 61 kg. It loses on output (4,500 W vs 7,200 W) and rated surge (8,000 W vs 14,400 W).

rivals.model: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (3,840 Wh, 6,000 W)
rivals.price: Sold out at ankersolix.com with no price shown, read 2026-11-15 (https://www.ankersolix.com/us/products/f3800-plus)
rivals.where_it_beats_ours: Expands to 53.8 kWh vs about 30 kWh. It loses on capacity, 240 V output (6,000 W), 120 V outlet output (2,400 W), solar input (3,200 W) and measured idle draw (80 W for the F3800, per The Solar Lab).
Much cheaper to start with. Arithmetic: $542/kWh vs $694/kWh. It loses on output (3,840 W vs 7,200 W) and capacity per box.
Same brand, cheaper per kWh (arithmetic: $530 vs $694) for homes that need only 120 V-level power

record.warranty: 5 years, per Jackery's Explorer 5000 Plus Basic Information page (https://faq.jackery.com/hc/en-us/articles/52303581495067-Explorer-5000-Plus-Basic-Information). Jackery's warranty terms also make battery-cell coverage depend on charging rules, and it sells an optional 2-year extension (https://www.jackery.com/pages/warranty-and-return).
record.summary: Jackery's largest single power station: 5,040 Wh of LiFePO4 and a 7,200 W split-phase 120/240 V inverter, expandable with up to five matching batteries. HOBOTECH measured 4.45 kWh usable and full rated output held at 240 V.
record.fit: Homeowners who need to run 240 V circuits such as a well pump or central AC through a transfer switch, especially with a large solar array.
caveats: High idle draw: about 58 W measured by The Solar Lab and 85 W by HOBOTECH (Jackery lists 50 W standby)
Struggled to start a 10,000 W-surge air conditioner in The Solar Lab's test
240 V charging needs Jackery's optional Smart Transfer Switch; 120 V wall charging measured at 1,750 W (HOBOTECH)
Weighs about 61 kg, and the extra batteries don't stack or roll with the unit (HOBOTECH)
The L14-50R outlet tops out at 7,200 W, which is 30 A at 240 V
